opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think "reasoning" is one of those words that gets thrown around a lot, and people mean very different things by it.

The way I tend to think about it is pretty pragmatic. Reasoning, for a language model, is basically the ability to spend more compute on a problem in a way that actually helps: to break something down, keep track of intermediate state, check itself, and arrive at an answer it couldn't have just pattern-matched in a single forward pass. That's why chain-of-thought was such a big deal early on. It wasn't magic, but it gave the model a scratchpad, a way to externalize the steps instead of jumping straight to the output.

What's changed recently is that we've moved from "prompt the model to think step by step" to actually training models to reason, with RL on verifiable tasks like math and code. The model learns, in some sense, *how* to use its thinking tokens: when to backtrack, when to try another approach, when to verify. That's a qualitative shift, because the reasoning behavior becomes something the model owns rather than something we coax out of it with clever prompting.

I'm a bit wary of the philosophical debates, like "is it *really* reasoning or just sophisticated pattern matching?" I don't find that framing super productive. If the model can reliably solve problems it hasn't seen, generalize to new domains, and get better when you give it more time to think, then for all practical purposes that's reasoning. The more interesting questions are about the edges: how well this transfers beyond domains with clean verifiers, how efficiently models use their thinking budget, and whether we're getting real generalization or just very good coverage of the training distribution.

So my short answer: reasoning is test-time compute used well. The exciting part is that we're only at the beginning of figuring out how to train for that properly.

r001.rationale: The response defines reasoning as using test-time compute effectively and describes RL as a way to train reasoning behavior. It does not characterize reasoning and reinforcement learning as nearly synonymous.

r002.rationale: The response discusses scratchpads and thinking tokens, but does not address whether latent thinking and discrete-token thinking are equivalent as an open question.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I'll say upfront that my view has shifted quite a bit over the years.

I think the first thing is that "reasoning" is kind of an overloaded word. People use it to mean very different things. There's the colloquial sense, like, does the model get the right answer on a math problem. And then there's the more mechanistic sense, like what is actually happening inside the model when it produces a chain of thought. And I think a lot of the confusion in the discourse comes from conflating those two.

My current take is that reasoning, at least in the way we're seeing it in today's models, is largely about giving the model more compute at inference time and a way to use it productively. When a model writes out a chain of thought, it's not that it has some separate reasoning module that switched on. It's that it's using the tokens as scratch space. Each token it generates is another forward pass, another chance to compute something, and the intermediate text is sort of a serialized form of that computation. So in a sense the chain of thought is the model externalizing its working memory.

What changed in the last couple of years is that we figured out how to train for this directly, with RL on verifiable rewards and so on, instead of just hoping it emerges from pretraining and prompting. And that turned out to matter a lot. The model learns things like when to backtrack, when to double check, when it's uncertain. Those are behaviors, and they're learnable, and they generalize more than I would have guessed.

But I'm also somewhat skeptical of the framing that this is "real" reasoning in some deep sense. I think the honest answer is that it's a pretty effective approximation. The models are still fundamentally doing next token prediction, and the reasoning traces are sometimes post hoc. There's good work showing that the written chain of thought doesn't always reflect what the model actually did to reach its answer. So I treat the traces as useful but not as ground truth about the model's internals.

The other thing I'd say is that I've become more of a data person over time. A lot of what looks like reasoning ability is downstream of what's in the pretraining mix and how much of it there is. You can have the fanciest RL setup in the world, but if the base model doesn't have the right priors, you're not going to get much out of it. So I think of reasoning as this layered thing. Pretraining gives you the raw material, and post training teaches the model how to allocate compute over that material.

So, short version: I think reasoning in today's models is real in the sense that it works and it generalizes, but it's probably better understood as learned inference time compute allocation than as some human-like faculty. And I think we're still pretty early in understanding it properly.

r001.rationale: The response describes reasoning as learned inference-time compute allocation and mentions RL as a way to train it; it does not characterize reasoning and reinforcement learning as nearly synonymous.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts written token traces with model internals, but does not identify whether latent thinking and discrete-token thinking are equivalent as an open question.

astra-6.text:
I think reasoning is a bit of an overloaded term. One way I think about it is: can the model take what it has learned and compose it to solve a problem it hasn’t seen before? That’s different from simply recalling an answer, although in practice it’s very difficult to separate the two.

There’s also a distinction between getting the answer right and producing a convincing explanation. A model can generate a very plausible chain of thought and still be wrong. So I wouldn’t treat the presence of intermediate steps as proof that it’s reasoning well. You want to ask whether those steps actually help it solve the problem, and whether that ability holds up when you change the problem a little.

What I find interesting is the role of computation. Instead of expecting a model to answer immediately, you can give it room to explore a solution, check it, and revise it. But more tokens don’t automatically mean better reasoning. The challenge is learning to use that additional computation productively.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reasoning as composing learned ideas and using additional computation, but it does not characterize reasoning and reinforcement learning as nearly synonymous.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss latent thinking versus discrete-token thinking or whether they are equivalent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reasoning is a bit of an overloaded term. Sometimes we mean the model getting a difficult question right, and sometimes we mean the process it uses to get there. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing. A model can produce a convincing explanation and still be wrong, so the explanation alone doesn’t establish that it reasoned correctly.

One useful way to think about it is computation: can the model use additional steps to break down a problem, check intermediate results, and revise an approach? Then the question becomes whether that extra computation reliably improves the answer, especially on problems that are different from what it has seen during training.

I wouldn’t draw a sharp boundary between pattern recognition and reasoning. Learning patterns can give you the building blocks for reasoning. The interesting question is how reliably the model can compose those building blocks when memorizing an answer isn’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reasoning as problem-solving and computation but does not characterize it as nearly synonymous with reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention latent thinking or discrete-token thinking, or frame their equivalence as an open question.
